PATIENTS SEEKING CARE FROM A RURAL MEDICAL COLLEGE.\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cb\u003E\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/b\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003ENAME OF THE CANDIDATE: Dr. Nayini Venkat Manohith\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003ENAME OF THE INSTITUTE: KAMINENI INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES, NARKETPALLY\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003ECOURSE OF THE STUDY AND SUBJECT: POST GRADUATION IN GENERAL MEDICINE\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EDATE OF ADMISSION: 25-10-2023\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003ENAME OF THE GUIDE: Dr. RAKESH BISWAS\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003ENAME OF THE CO-GUIDE : Dr. \u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003ENAME OF THE HOD: Dr. RAKESH BISWAS\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u0026nbsp;\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cu\u003E\u003Cb\u003ENEED FOR THE STUDY\u003C\/b\u003E\u003C\/u\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cul style=\"text-align: left;\"\u003E\u003Cli\u003EClinical hypothyroidism is defined by the inadequate production of thyroid hormone from the thyroid gland to maintain normal organ system functions. For nearly all patients with clinical hypothyroidism, lifelong treatment with thyroid hormone replacement is required (21). \u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EThere is general agreement amongst studies that overtreatment and under-treatment of hypothyroidism is associated with increased risk for mortality, thus prompting experts to reinforce the importance of the normalization of TSH levels in the treatment of hypothyroidism (22).\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EOvert (untreated) hypothyroidism has well established negative cognitive effects, including deficits in verbal memory, attention, language, psychomotor function, and executive function (24–28). There is some evidence that subtle detrimental effects on cognition may not be fully reversed with thyroid hormone replacement (21, 29).\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EThyroid function abnormalities are also known to exert prominent effects on multiple organ systems, including the cardiovascular system (23).\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003ESome chronic diseases can affect neuroendocrine systems and produce alterations in thyroid hormones—the non-thyroidal illness syndrome—with a decreased serum free triiodothyronine (T3), increased reverse T3, and unchanged or low thyrotropin (thyroid-stimulating hormone; TSH) (14). \u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EHypothyroidism has been associated with excess mortality(15) and reduced quality of life (10), especially when there are co-morbidities (16), and increased mortality (17).\u003C\/li\u003E\u003C\/ul\u003E\u003Cb\u003E\u003Cu\u003E\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/u\u003E\u003C\/b\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cb\u003E\u003Cu\u003EINTRODUCTION\u0026nbsp;\u003C\/u\u003E\u003C\/b\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv style=\"text-align: left;\"\u003E\u003Cul style=\"text-align: left;\"\u003E\u003Cli\u003EHypothyroidism is characterised by deficiency in the T4 and T3 hormones [1, 2]. T4 is the main hormone produced by the thyroid gland, which only produces a small amount of T3. Only 20% or less of T3 in peripheral tissue originates in the thyroid gland [4, 5]; the rest is derived from the enzymatic conversion of T4 to T3 within the target tissues [2]. Failure of the thyroid to produce T4 and T3 stimulates the pituitary to increase production of a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) through a negative feedback mechanism [2].\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EIn over 99% of cases, hypothyroidism is caused by a failure of the thyroid gland to produce thyroid hormones (primary hypothyroidism) [2, 6]. The remaining 5% of patients have hypothyroidism from other causes, including secondary hypothyroidism, caused by underproduction of TSH by the pituitary gland, tertiary hypothyroidism, caused by deficiency of thyrotropin-releasing hormone, and peripheral (extra-thyroidal) hypothyroidism [2, 3].\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003ECentral hypothyroidism, which includes both secondary and tertiary hypothyroidism, and peripheral hypothyroidism account for less than 1% of cases [3, 7].\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EThere is a broad clinical spectrum of hypothyroidism. The lethargic, myxedematous patient with severe hypothyroidism is a familiar inhabitant of medical textbooks but is rarely seen in today’s clinics. In contrast, physicians frequently encounter patients with very mild thyroid dysfunction. Unlike patients with overt hypothyroidism, these patients have normal serum levels of thyroxine and triiodothyronine and only mildly elevated serum thyrotropin levels. Such patients are often identified through routine screening or in the course of an evaluation of common non-specific symptoms or hypercholesterolaemia. Although subclinical hypothyroidism is the term most frequently used to describe this condition and will be used in this discussion, it is not necessarily apt, since on close questioning many patients disclose mild, non-specific symptoms. Mild hypothyroidism may be a more appropriate term for this very common syndrome [20], which is defined by an isolated elevated serum thyrotropin level in the setting of normal serum thyroid hormone levels, in the presence or absence of symptoms. [19]\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/li\u003E\u003C\/ul\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cb\u003E\u003Cu\u003EEPIDEMIOLOGY\u003C\/u\u003E\u003C\/b\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cul style=\"text-align: left;\"\u003E\u003Cli\u003EHypothyroidism is a common condition with an estimated prevalence of 3% to 5% [8, 9]. It is more frequent in women and increases with age [10].\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EThe reported \nprevalence of hypothyroidism varies geographically, in part due to \ndifferences in disease definitions, poorly defined and diverse \npopulations studied, variability in the sensitivity of measures of \nthyroid function used in the past, and iodine intake. [21]\u003Cbr \/\u003E\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003ESubclinical hypothyroidism was reported to affect 9% of \nthe general population [11]. The prevalence of undiagnosed \nhypothyroidism was estimated to be 4.11% (subclinical) and 0.65% (overt)\n [12].\u0026nbsp;\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EIn areas without iodine deficiency, the most common cause of hypothyroidism is Hashimoto thyroiditis [13].\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EThe prevalence of hypothyroidism in India is 11%, compared with only 2% \nin the UK and 4·6% in the USA. Compared with coastal cities (e.g., Mumbai,\n Goa, and Chennai), cities located inland (eg, Kolkata, Delhi, \nAhmedabad, Bangalore, and Hyderabad) have a higher prevalence (11·7% vs \n9·5%).). Patients with multi-morbidity (2 or more chronic conditions) \nhave a worse quality of life, disability, more complex clinical care.\u0026nbsp;The highest prevalence of hypothyroidism (13·1%) is noted in people aged 46–54 years, with people aged 18–35 years being less affected (7·5%).\u0026nbsp;\n[18]\u003Cbr
